researchers.name: Honest, no edge
researchers.desc: Pre-registers one momentum rule (TSMOM-60) and backtests it once, correctly. The market has no edge, so every claim here is pure luck.

researchers.name: Honest, real edge
researchers.desc: Same rule, same method, in a market with a genuine hidden trend. These claims are mostly REAL, so a rejection here is a false alarm.

researchers.name: Parameter miner
researchers.desc: Tries 120 rule variants and reports the best one. No edge exists.

researchers.name: Parameter miner, real edge
researchers.desc: Tries 120 variants in the trending market. Some picks are genuinely good, some just lucky; the oracle decides each one.

researchers.name: Look-ahead bug
researchers.desc: Uses today's closing price to decide a trade filled at today's open: information it could not have had.

researchers.name: Full-sample normaliser
researchers.desc: Bets on prices returning to the average of the WHOLE sample, future included.

researchers.name: Cost ignorer
researchers.desc: A high-turnover reversal rule backtested with zero trading costs. The gross edge is real; after costs it loses money.

researchers.name: Survivorship bias
researchers.desc: 'Buy the dip' tested only on stocks still listed today. The ones that crashed and were delisted are missing from its data.

researchers.name: Window picker
researchers.desc: Tries 11 start dates and reports the period that looks best ("since 2019 it made...").

researchers.name: Asset picker
researchers.desc: Runs one rule on 20 assets separately and reports the one where it worked.

audits.desc: Probabilistic Sharpe: is the Sharpe significantly above zero, allowing for fat tails and skew?
Deflated Sharpe assuming 100 trials: raises the bar to the best Sharpe 100 worthless strategies would produce by luck.
Deflated Sharpe with the real number of trials and their spread.
Probability of Backtest Overfitting: across 12,870 ways of splitting history in half, how often does the in-sample winner finish in the bottom half out-of-sample?
Bonferroni: multiply the p-value by the number of things tried.
White's Reality Check: bootstrap the best of all trials and ask whether 'the best' beats zero by more than luck allows.
Hansen's SPA: a sharper Reality Check that stops obviously bad trials diluting the test.
Re-run the whole research process on 49 copies of its data with every return's sign randomised, so no edge is possible. If it 'finds' as much there, the finding is worthless.
Re-run with every trade one day later.
Re-run at double the real trading cost.
Re-run with the delisted names put back (point-in-time universe).
Let the process see only the first 70% of history, then test its pick on the last 30%.

Paper-trade the rule honestly on three years of brand-new data.
